summary: For 10–11 year olds learning the human circulatory system (UK DfE Y6; note NGSS places this at middle school, MS-LS1-3, with no US elementary performance expectation naming heart/vessels/blood). The core objective: name the main parts (heart, arteries, veins, capillaries, blood), describe their functions, and grasp that blood CIRCULATES in a continuous refreshed loop (e.g. body→heart→lungs→heart→body) rather than travelling one way and being 'used up'. Anchor the abstract model to the child's own body (pulse, heartbeat, quickening after exercise), name vessels by direction so labels carry function, and keep double circulation simple (blood passes through the heart on the way to the body and again after the lungs); chambers, valves and the full double circuit are for later (KS3).
misconceptions: Thinking blood travels one way and gets 'used up', rather than circulating in a continuous refreshed loop.
Believing the heart is on the far left of the chest or is heart-shaped, rather than roughly central and fist-sized.
Assuming blood in veins is actually blue (it is dark red); the blue is only a diagram convention and skin/vein appearance.
Confusing arteries and veins, or thinking arteries always carry oxygen-rich blood (the pulmonary artery does not).
Thinking the heart is a single pump with one path, missing that it sends blood both to the lungs and to the body.

activities.title: Drive the circulation loop
steps: Power a circulation-loop model by repeatedly tapping/pumping the heart so a surge of bright-red (oxygen-rich) blood flows out through the arteries to the body.

Follow a single blood 'parcel': watch it drop off oxygen, nutrients and water and collect carbon dioxide/waste at the body cells, turn blue (oxygen-poor), flow back through the veins to the heart, get pumped to the lungs, release the carbon dioxide and pick up oxygen so it flushes back to red, then start the loop again.
Tap each vessel to label it: arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins return it, capillaries are the tiny vessels where exchange with cells happens.
Toggle a 'rest vs run' control to make the heart beat faster and the flow speed up, then relate this to how your own heart behaves during exercise.
activities.insight: Blood goes ROUND in a continuous, closed loop and is refreshed at the lungs — it is not consumed on a one-way trip. As it circulates it both delivers (oxygen, nutrients, water) and collects (carbon dioxide, waste). The heart pumps blood both to the lungs and to the body; vessel names describe direction and function.

activities.title: Feel your own pump (pulse and prediction)
steps: Find your pulse at the wrist or neck. Before feeling it, predict: does blood leave the heart in a smooth steady stream or in pushes, and why?
Feel the throb with each heartbeat and compare it to your prediction.
Do star jumps or run on the spot, then feel your pulse again and describe what changed.
State in your own words what the heartbeat is doing to the blood and why exercise changes it.
activities.insight: The heart pumps blood in beats to drive it around the loop; 'the heart pumps blood' becomes a felt fact, and the rate rises with exercise to move more blood (and oxygen) to working muscles.

activities.title: Name the parts and bust the myths
steps: Match each part (heart, artery, vein, capillary, blood) to its job.
Explain why blood keeps going round instead of stopping, and list what blood carries (oxygen, nutrients and water delivered to cells; carbon dioxide and other waste carried away from them).
Decide whether this statement is true: 'the blood in your veins is blue' — and explain your answer.

Locate roughly where the heart sits (near the middle of the chest behind the breastbone, tilted slightly to the left, about fist-sized), correcting the idea that it is on the far left or heart-shaped.
activities.insight: Each vessel's name carries its function; blood is a two-way carrier (delivers and collects); the blue colouring is only a convention, and the heart's real position and size differ from common myths.

activities.title: Order the journey and check understanding
steps: Put the blood's route in order: body → heart → lungs (collect oxygen) → heart → body.

Answer: if blood isn't used up, how does the same blood keep delivering oxygen all day? By what route does it get from your toes back to your heart? Besides oxygen, what else is it carrying as it passes your toes? Where does it pick up fresh oxygen?
Choose the correct statement and explain why 'blood only travels one way and gets used up' is wrong.
Describe the heart's job as pumping (not making) blood, noting blood cells are produced in bone marrow.
activities.insight: The route forms a closed, continuous loop; the heart pumps and does not manufacture blood; capillaries link arteries to veins where exchange happens.

activities.title: Enrichment: explore the heart in three dimensions
steps: Examine a rotatable/cutaway model of the heart to see the left and right sides and how the great vessels connect.
Relate the left/right sides to the idea that the heart pumps blood to the lungs AND to the body.
activities.insight: The heart is a genuinely three-dimensional muscular double pump with left and right sides feeding two destinations (lungs and body).

checkQuestion: Blood leaves your heart and travels all the way out to your toes. What happens to that blood after it has delivered oxygen to your toes — does it get used up so the heart has to make new blood, or does something else happen? And what is the heart's actual job in all this?
checkAnswer: The blood is not used up. After delivering oxygen it returns to the heart through the veins, is pumped to the lungs to pick up more oxygen, and circulates again in a continuous loop. The heart's job is to pump blood, not to make it — blood cells are produced in bone marrow.
